statement: Change of variables (integration by substitution): given g:[a,b]→I differentiable with continuous derivative, and f:I→ℝ continuous, setting u = g(x) (so du = g'(x) dx) converts one integral into another: ∫_a^b f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du. For indefinite integrals the corresponding identity is ∫ f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du, with u = g(x) substituted back into the result afterward.

symbols.meaning: differentiable function [a,b] → I defining the substitution
continuous function on I being integrated
transformed limits of integration in u
differential of u, equal to g'(x) dx

properties.property: For definite integrals, the bounds transform along with the variable: ∫_a^b f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du, so no back-substitution into x is needed.
properties.why: the limits a, b are values of x, and after substitution the integral is expressed in u, so its limits must be the corresponding u-values g(a), g(b)

properties.property: For indefinite integrals, ∫ f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du, and after evaluating the right side, u must be replaced back by g(x) to express the antiderivative in the original variable.
properties.why: an indefinite integral has no bounds to carry the change of variable, so the result must be re-expressed in x explicitly

properties.property: The differential relation du = g'(x) dx follows from treating du/dx = g'(x) heuristically as a ratio of infinitesimals; this is what licenses replacing g'(x) dx by du under the integral sign.
properties.why: this is the informal justification given for the substitution before the rigorous proof via the fundamental theorem of calculus

properties.property: The formula can be applied in either direction: reading left-to-right (u = g(x), 'u-substitution') to simplify a composite integrand, or right-to-left (x = h(u), e.g. trigonometric substitution) to introduce a new variable that simplifies the integrand.
properties.why: the source states the identity is symmetric and can be read either way depending on which side is easier to compute

assumptions.assumption: g is differentiable on [a,b] with continuous derivative g', and f is continuous on an interval I containing the range of g
assumptions.breaks_when: g' fails to be continuous, g is not differentiable at some point, or f is discontinuous on the range of g

assumptions.assumption: the integrand can be factored as f(g(x))·g'(x), i.e. the derivative of the inner function (up to a constant) appears as a multiplicative factor
assumptions.breaks_when: no such factor g'(x) is present in the integrand, making the substitution inapplicable without further manipulation

failure_modes.mode: wrong numerical value for a definite integral
failure_modes.signature: the evaluated integral is a constant multiple or otherwise off from the correct value
failure_modes.cause: substituting u = g(x) in a definite integral but forgetting to change the limits of integration from a, b to g(a), g(b)

failure_modes.mode: answer left in the wrong variable
failure_modes.signature: an indefinite integral's final antiderivative still contains u instead of x
failure_modes.cause: omitting the back-substitution u → g(x) after integrating in u

failure_modes.mode: substitution does not simplify the integral
failure_modes.signature: after substitution, the integrand still contains x mixed with u, or g'(x) cannot be isolated
failure_modes.cause: the chosen substitution's derivative g'(x) does not match (up to constant factor) a term actually present in the integrand
